title: No Slaughterhouses, No Oversight: The Full Scale of Vietnam's Food Safety Gap
excerpt: The complete absence of registered dog meat slaughterhouses creates an untracked, uninspected supply chain operating in plain sight — and what it would take to change that.
body_html:
In every formal food sector in Vietnam, there is a regulatory baseline: registered facilities, inspection regimes, sanitation standards. The dog meat trade has none of these. There is not a single registered dog meat slaughterhouse in Vietnam — a fact confirmed by food safety authorities in Ho Chi Minh City.

This creates a food safety gap with no equivalent in the formal meat sector. Animals enter the supply chain with no health screening. Slaughter occurs in uncontrolled environments. Meat is handled and distributed without cold chain management or pathogen testing. Consumers have no way to assess the safety of what they are consuming.

The comparison to countries that have enacted bans is instructive. The Philippines banned the dog meat trade in 1998 under the Animal Welfare Act, and South Korea has been progressively restricting it through legislation. In both cases, the regulatory argument — food safety, public health, disease control — was as central as animal welfare in driving legislative change.

Vietnam has the public mandate to act. 95% of Vietnamese respondents support ending this trade. What is missing is political will and formal enforcement mechanisms. A petition directed at the Communist Party and food safety authorities is the most direct way to close that gap.

Add your signature and demand the regulatory oversight that protects public health.
author: SDE Research Team
